Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I was betrayed by someone I trusted

issues.explanation: Fire/flames is not a plausible primary trigger for childhood physical abuse by a caregiver unless other profile elements indicate fire-related abuse or a fire context, which they do not. The rest of the trigger, threat, memory, and appraisal items point to interpersonal threat rather than burn/fire trauma, so this item is hard to reconcile with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: Survival guilt about others dying is difficult to reconcile with childhood physical abuse by a caregiver when no other items reference deaths, fatalities, or witnessing others die. It also conflicts with the rest of the profile, which centers on helplessness and failure to stop abuse rather than surviving when others did not.

vignette: Eleanor Vance grew up in a quiet New England house where the air always seemed to hold its breath. Her caregiver's moods were a shifting landscape; one moment he would read to her by the fireplace, the next he would snap over a misplaced book or an unanswered question. She remembered the afternoon he struck her after she spilled tea on the rug, his sudden lunge freezing her in the hallway. What terrified her most was not just the violence, but the way he would promise to make it right before turning cold again. Years later, standing alone with a male contractor in her kitchen, or attending a friend's funeral in a quiet cemetery, the ground felt just as unstable. The uncertainty of how he would react, the solemn weight of grief, and the isolation with another man all carried the same invisible threat: that trust could vanish in an instant, leaving her exposed. As Eleanor matured, the house's unpredictability rewired her nervous system. When a colleague raised his voice during a deadline review, or when a sudden knock came at her door, her body would brace before her mind could even register the context. She spent years trying to quiet the constant low hum of watchfulness, yet every new ambiguity in her schedule felt like a spark in a dry field. Encountering these moments pulled the past into sharp relief. The scene of the rug, his belt, and her own frozen posture surfaced with the clarity of slides projected onto her retinas, even when she found herself staring at a spreadsheet, unable to find words to explain why her chest tightened so suddenly. Confronted with these relentless reminders, Eleanor began to convince herself that she was fundamentally powerless to steer her own life, and that she would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. Over the decades, these internal shifts calcified into habits that reshaped her daily life. Working as a QA engineer required her to scrutinize systems for flaws, a task that mirrored her relentless search for safety. Yet her insistence on avoiding unscheduled meetings with male supervisors and her refusal to navigate cemeteries without a companion slowly isolated her at work. When she caught herself holding her breath during a vendor call, or when her shoulders locked at a partner's quick shift in posture, the physical alarm never ceased to fuel her core beliefs. Each time her nerves flared without cause, Eleanor interpreted it as proof that the world remained fundamentally dangerous and that she would never be able to prevent harm from reaching her again. The memories of that childhood helplessness would not fade; instead, they would deepen her conviction that she had betrayed herself by surviving passively. She would sit in her study, certain that she would never forgive herself for the years she lost, and the shame of that inaction would instantly make the prospect of stepping outside feel like walking into a trap. For years, Eleanor managed her life by strictly controlling her environment, yet the more she restricted her movements, the heavier the invisible weight grew. When her husband gently suggested they attend his sister's memorial service, her throat closed around the word yes. She had come to believe that any lapse in vigilance would invite the same helplessness she had known as a child, and that the memories of the abuse would only grow more vivid, leaving her emotionally hollow before the shock returned. The constant state of guard, the photographic intrusions, and the crushing belief that she was fundamentally unrescued wove together into a seamless circuit. She would wake at three in the morning, heart hammering, convinced that her body's readiness for violence was the only evidence that danger was still waiting. This relentless feedback kept her trapped in the aftermath, until the sheer exhaustion of carrying the shame finally compelled her to sit across from a therapist. She did not know if she would ever forgive herself for the years she lost to fear, but she was hoping, against every instinct, to learn how to trust the ground beneath her feet again.
